title: The Declaration of Independence Was Once Breaking News—and a Woman Risked Everything to Print It
summary:
Today, the Declaration of Independence is enshrined at the National Archives, sealed in a titanium frame behind bulletproof glass. But in the summer of 1776, it was a radical, untested proclamation hurtling through a fragile communications network. Historian Emily Sneff's new book, When the Declaration of Independence Was News, reconstructs those chaotic early days, revealing that the document we revere was initially "malleable, easily combined with other pieces of information and misinformation."

On July 4, 1776, after Congress adopted the text, Philadelphia printer John Dunlap worked through the night to produce the first broadsides—poster-sized sheets with the Declaration set in a single wide column. These were dispatched by horseback to state assemblies, military commanders, and local leaders. Newspapers reprinted them, and public readings drew crowds to courthouses and churches. But the signed parchment we picture didn't exist yet; signing began on August 2, and by then, most colonists had already learned of independence through these printed copies.

Sneff emphasizes the materiality of these early versions. No two were exactly alike. Printers in different colonies made aesthetic and grammatical tweaks. A Boston merchant scribbled annotations linking grievances to earlier newspaper articles. Anglican ministers marked up copies as they wrestled with how to shift their sermons away from royal sovereignty. An estimated 125 Dunlap broadsides survive today, but many more were lost to time, confiscated, or thrown overboard from ships.

The most striking figure in this story is Mary Katharine Goddard. In July 1776, she printed the Declaration in her Baltimore newspaper, signing it only as "M.K. Goddard." But in January 1777, after Congress fled to Baltimore, they asked her to print the first broadsides that included the signers' names. This time, she boldly used her full name at the bottom—making her the only woman to print the Declaration under her own name during the war. It was an act of immense courage; the British considered the document treasonous, and Goddard was putting herself directly in the crosshairs.

Sneff notes that January 1777 marks the transition of the Declaration from a news item to an archival treasure. Goddard's version, with its two-column layout and capitalized religious references like "God" and "Divine Providence," became a bridge between the messy, urgent news of revolution and the polished symbol we know today. Her story reminds us that the founding documents were not handed down by gods but were produced by real people taking real risks.
why_it_matters: This story shows teenagers that the iconic documents they study were once uncertain, contested pieces of breaking news. It highlights how ordinary people—including a woman who defied gender roles—took real risks to shape the nation's founding. Understanding this messy, human process can make history feel more relatable and inspire critical thinking about how 'official' narratives come to be.

background_read: The Declaration of Independence was not always the sacred object we see today. In 1776, the Second Continental Congress voted to break from Britain, but the document was primarily distributed through printed sheets called broadsides. The famous engrossed parchment with signatures—now housed at the National Archives in Washington, D.C.—wasn't created until later. John Dunlap, a Philadelphia printer, ran off about 200 copies on July 4–5, which riders carried to the colonies. These first versions were considered treasonous by the British; anyone caught with them could be executed.

Mary Katharine Goddard was a remarkable figure: a Baltimore postmaster and printer who ran her late brother's newspaper, the Maryland Journal. By printing the Declaration with the signers' names in January 1777 and identifying herself as the printer, she took an enormous risk. Women in printing were rare, and her boldness made her a target not only for the British but also for those who thought a woman shouldn't be in such a public role. Later, she was controversially removed from her postmaster position—some historians suggest gender bias played a part.

Emily Sneff is a historian of the American Revolution who studies how the Declaration spread and evolved. Her work highlights that the document's meaning was not fixed from the start; communities read it aloud, newspapers edited it, and ministers interpreted it in sermons. This messy, irregular process is a far cry from the marble halls of the National Archives, reminding us that the founding ideals were once breaking news—imperfect, urgent, and alive.

perspectives.description: Goddard's bold decision to print her full name on a treasonous document reveals the quiet heroism behind the Revolution. Her story elevates the role of printers and women in nation-building, showing that independence was not just a political act but a community effort. This perspective celebrates the everyday courage that makes democratic ideals possible, giving forgotten figures their due in history.

The article hints at the risks by mentioning Goddard put herself 'in the crosshairs,' but it doesn't dwell on the consequences she faced, such as being removed from her postmaster role. A critical view might argue that even brave acts were often punished within a system that devalued women's contributions. Over time, the tidy, polished narrative of independence can erase the real harms suffered by those who stuck their necks out, especially minority voices.

Sneff's research highlights how a document transitions from mere news to an archival treasure—a process of canonization. The analysis shows that early versions were not uniform; printers' edits and readers' annotations made each copy unique. This reflects larger patterns in how societies construct historical significance: messy, contingent events are later sanitized into a single, authoritative version. The Declaration's journey from broadside to bulletproof glass is a case study in collective memory shaping.

If more attention is paid to the material history—like the annotated broadsides—schools and museums might shift how they teach the Revolution. Emphasizing the unpredictability and the diverse people involved could inspire young people to see themselves as potential agents of change, even in messy circumstances. In the future, digital archives and new scholarship may recover even more stories of printers, messengers, and ordinary citizens whose small acts made the big moment possible, challenging the myth of a handful of great men alone.
